rationale: B wins because it keeps the strongest angles clean, proof-gated, and reporter-shaped. Its headline “Going's new AI planner lets the airfare pick the destination” finds the real product-design story without pretending the company invented travel AI. A has useful bones, but “how Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products” smuggles in unsupplied competitor context and then builds too much on it. B's line “there is no drafting step that fixes a missing number” is exactly the adult in the room.
gaps_in_A: “how Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products” is not in the update; named competitor context needs evidence before it becomes the frame.
“different from everyone else already building the same feature” overclaims the differentiation. The update supports fare-alert-triggered planning, not category uniqueness.
“The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app” is padded profile bait. The former name is context, not enough story by itself.
“A tech reporter or columnist” is too vague, and the “AI will handle your whole trip end-to-end” narrative is asserted before it is proven.
gaps_in_B: “now gates its first AI feature to Premium” invents “first.” The update says this planner is launching, not that Going has never shipped AI before.
“Most trip-planning tools start from a destination” is plausible, but still an unsupported category claim. It needs a quick proof point before pitching.
“the company's own phrasing says ‘yet’” overreads the supplied wording. “Yet” signals a possible roadmap question, not a company admission.
“category-creation” is a little puffed up. This is a strong product-design angle, not category creation unless the market evidence backs it.
